title: Étale local identification of regular boundary components with coordinate hyperplanes
statement: Let $X$ be a locally Noetherian scheme [pqf-def-locnoeth] and let $D\hookrightarrow X$ be a reduced closed subscheme [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Suppose that $D_1,\ldots,D_m$ are exactly the distinct irreducible components of $D$ [def-weil-irreducible-components], each with its reduced induced scheme structure, and that every $D_a$ is regular [def-weil-regular-scheme]. Let $v:W\to X$ be étale [def-weil-etale-morphism], let $w\in W$, and set $x=v(w)$. Assume that $R=\mathcal O_{W,w}$ is a regular local ring of dimension $d$, and choose a regular system of parameters $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ [def-weil-pbc-regular-system-of-parameters], meaning $d$ elements generating the maximal ideal of $R$. Choose regular functions representing these germs on an open neighborhood $V$ of $w$. For $0\le r\le d$, suppose that $D\times_X V=V(t_1\cdots t_r)$ as closed subschemes of $V$ (the empty product is $1$). Here the coordinate hyperplane with index $i$ means the closed subscheme $V(t_i)\subset V$. Then, after shrinking $V$ around $w$, there is a bijection $\{a:x\in D_a\}\simeq\{1,\ldots,r\}$, written $a\mapsto i(a)$, such that $D_a\times_X V=V(t_{i(a)})$ for every $a$ with $x\in D_a$; for all other $a$ the pullback is empty. Consequently every scheme-theoretic intersection of selected $D_a$ pulls back to the intersection of their assigned coordinate hyperplanes, or is empty if a selected component misses $x$. Every generic point of a nonempty irreducible component of $D_a\times_XW$ maps to the generic point of $D_a$.

proof.text: Discard from $V$ the inverse images of the finitely many $D_a$ missing $x$; these are closed and miss $w$. Put $A=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ and let $I\subset A$ be the ideal of $D$ and $\mathfrak p_a\subset A$ the ideal of $D_a$ for $x\in D_a$. The $\mathfrak p_a$ are exactly the distinct minimal primes over $I$: in an affine neighbourhood, irreducible closed subsets are $V(\mathfrak p)$, and maximality among irreducible subsets of $V(I)$ is minimality of the prime over $I$; localization retains precisely the components containing $x$. Since each $D_a$ is reduced, its defining ideal is this prime, rather than a thickening. The closed-immersion affine description identifies $\mathcal O_{D_a,x}=A/\mathfrak p_a$ and the local pullback at $w$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(R/\mathfrak p_aR)$.

source.place: Expose VIII, Remark 4.2.2(i): distinct reduced irreducible boundary components; elementary affine/local translation

proof.text: For each retained $a$, the morphism $E_a=D_a\times_X W\to D_a$ is étale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change], hence smooth by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-smooth-zero-dimensional-fibres]. Choose a regular affine neighbourhood of $x$ in $D_a$, and an affine neighbourhood of the point $(x,w)$ in its inverse image. By the affine-local meaning of smoothness in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], the induced ring map $C\to B$ is smooth, with $C$ Noetherian regular. By [lem-weil-pbc-regular-ring-smooth-ascent], $B$ is regular. The definition of regularity therefore makes its local ring $R/\mathfrak p_aR$ regular local. By [lem-sc-regular-local-domain] this is a nonzero domain, so $\mathfrak q_a=\mathfrak p_aR$ is a proper prime ideal of $R$.

source.place: Tag 07NF, lemma-regular-goes-up; Morphisms Tags 02GO, lemma-base-change-etale, and 02GK, lemma-etale-smooth-unramified; regular local domains: Tag 00NP, lemma-regular-domain

proof.text: The map $A/\mathfrak p_a\to R/\mathfrak q_a$ is flat: it is the stalk map of the étale morphism $E_a\to D_a$ from Step 2, using [def-weil-etale-morphism] and [def-weil-flat-morphism]. Both rings are domains, the source because it is a local ring of the regular scheme $D_a$, by [lem-sc-regular-local-domain]. Let $\mathfrak k$ be the contraction of the zero prime of $R/\mathfrak q_a$. Apply [lem-sc-flat-going-down] to the primes $(0)\subseteq\mathfrak k$ and the upstairs prime $(0)$. The supplied prime below $(0)$ can only be $(0)$, so $\mathfrak k=(0)$. Thus $\mathfrak q_a\cap A=\mathfrak p_a$. In particular, distinct $a$ give distinct $\mathfrak q_a$.

source.place: Tag 00HS, lemma-flat-going-down, applied to the zero prime; Tag 00NP, lemma-regular-domain

proof.text: Put $T=t_1\cdots t_r$. By [lem-trf-regular-local-ufd-boundary-factorization], each $t_i$ is prime, so $P_i=(t_i)$ is a proper prime ideal. By [lem-weil-pbc-regular-local-cotangent-dimension], $\mathfrak m_R/\mathfrak m_R^2$ has dimension $d$. The $d$ parameters generate $\mathfrak m_R$, so their images span this $d$-dimensional vector space and form a basis. Consequently $P_i\subseteq P_j$ forces $i=j$: an equation $t_i=ct_j$ gives proportional cotangent classes, impossible for two different basis vectors. Every prime containing $T$ contains some $t_i$. Therefore the $P_i$, $1\le i\le r$, are exactly the minimal primes over $(T)$, and are pairwise incomparable. For $r=0$, $T=1$ and there is no such prime.

source.place: Tag 0AG0, lemma-regular-local-UFD, proof opening: parameters are prime; Algebra Tag 00KU, definition-regular-local and preceding cotangent-space discussion

proof.text: The underlying set of $D$ is the union of the $D_a$. Taking inverse images in $\operatorname{Spec}R$ gives $V(T)=\bigcup_aV(\mathfrak q_a)$, and each $\mathfrak q_a$ contains $T$. For every $i$, the point $P_i$ therefore belongs to some $V(\mathfrak q_a)$, so $\mathfrak q_a\subseteq P_i$. Since $\mathfrak q_a$ is prime and contains $T$, it contains some $P_j$. The incomparability from Step 4 forces $j=i$, and hence $\mathfrak q_a=P_i$. This uses the inverse image of a finite union of closed sets; it does not presume that pulling back a reduced union is reduced.

source.place: Expose VIII, Remark 4.2.2(i) and Lemma 4.2.9: elementary comparison of the boundary components in a parameter-product chart

proof.text: Conversely fix $a$. Primality and $T\in\mathfrak q_a$ give $P_i\subseteq\mathfrak q_a$ for some $i$. Step 5 gives $b$ with $P_i=\mathfrak q_b$. Contracting to $A$ using Step 3 gives $\mathfrak p_b\subseteq\mathfrak p_a$. Since these are distinct minimal primes over $I$, they must be equal and $b=a$. Thus $\mathfrak q_a=P_i$. Distinct $a$ give distinct primes by Step 3, and distinct $i$ give distinct primes by Step 4; Step 5 supplies all $i$. This is the desired bijection at the local ring. If $r=0$, every retained $a$ would give a proper prime containing $1$, a contradiction, so both indexing sets are empty.

source.place: Expose VIII, Remark 4.2.2(i): elementary minimal-prime argument identifying individual components

proof.text: Shrink $V$ to an affine neighbourhood $\operatorname{Spec}B$ of $w$, with prime $\mathfrak n$ corresponding to $w$. Since $W\to X$ is étale, it is locally of finite presentation and thus locally of finite type; [pqf-lem-locnoeth-lft] makes $W$ locally Noetherian. Thus $B$ is Noetherian. For a retained $a$, let $K_a\subset B$ define $D_a\times_X V$; Step 6 says $(K_a)_{\mathfrak n}=(t_{i(a)})_{\mathfrak n}$. Choose finite generators $k_1,\ldots,k_s$ of $K_a$. For every $j$, localization membership supplies $u_j\notin\mathfrak n$ with $u_jk_j\in(t_{i(a)})$; the reverse membership supplies $u_0\notin\mathfrak n$ with $u_0t_{i(a)}\in K_a$. On $D(u_0\cdots u_s)$ the ideals coincide. Intersect these finitely many principal neighbourhoods for all $a$. This proves equality of the closed subschemes, and preserves the empty pullbacks removed in Step 1.

source.place: Tag 01T6, lemma-finite-type-noetherian, and elementary finite-generator localization argument; closed immersions: Tag 01QO, lemma-closed-immersion; the local spreading principle is also illustrated by Coherent Tag 01Y3

proof.text: Scheme-theoretic intersection is a fibre product of the closed immersions. By the fibre-product universal property, pulling it back along $V\to X$ gives the intersection of their pullbacks. On an affine chart the intersection of closed subschemes with ideals $K_a$ has ideal $\sum_aK_a$: both describe maps on which every $K_a$ vanishes. Step 7 therefore gives the ideal $(t_{i(a)}:a\text{ selected})$. If one selected component misses $x$, its pulled-back ideal is the unit ideal, so the intersection is empty. For an empty selection the intersection is $V$ itself, as required.

source.place: Expose VIII, Remark 4.2.2(i): scheme-theoretic intersections; elementary quotient-ring universal property

proof.text: Finally let $z$ be the generic point of an irreducible component of $D_a\times_X W$. The projection to $D_a$ is étale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-scheme-base-change], hence flat by [def-weil-etale-morphism]. Choose an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}C$ of $D_a$ around its image and an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}B$ around $z$ mapping into it. The ring $C$ is a domain because $D_a$ is reduced and irreducible, hence integral by [def-pc-integral-scheme]. The map $C\to B$ is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-morphism-affine-criterion]. The point $z$ corresponds to a minimal prime $Q$ of $B$: a larger irreducible closed subset would contradict that its closure is a component. Put $P=Q\cap C$. Going down [lem-sc-flat-going-down] lifts $(0)\subseteq P$ to a prime $Q_0\subseteq Q$ contracting to zero. Minimality forces $Q_0=Q$, hence $P=(0)$. Thus the image of $z$ is the generic point of this nonempty affine open, and hence the generic point of the irreducible scheme $D_a$. This argument applies on all of $W$, independently of the shrinking used for the coordinate identification.
